entries.title: Finding the right fit for the next House speaker
entries.summary: <p>Four House Democrats who were instrumental in drafting and circulating a letter last week that successfully called for a new Illinois House speaker issued another letter the next day aimed partly at the now-departing chamber leader and his internal organization: Back off.</p><p>After noting that House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch had helpfully <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/05/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-mutiny-26-democrats-call-for-new-leader-harry-benton-scandal" >folded his tent </a>quickly and dropped out of the race, the letter pointed out that Democrats now have lots of time for a “deliberate and intentional” process of selecting the new chamber leader. Reps. Mary Beth Canty, D-Arlington Heights; Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago; Tracy Katz Muhl, D-Northbrook; and Larry Walsh, D-Elwood, sent the new letter.</p><p>The one thing the four definitely do not want is interference from Welch and those around him.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3d0000" name="module-3d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>“We must ensure our next Speaker is able to take the time necessary to earn the support of our caucus members, without interference or a finger on the scale from the current Speaker’s operation,” the four warned.</p><p>Rumors have been flying lately about Welch lining up a successor. The four letter persons do not want a repeat of the behind the scenes handoff that moved the speaker’s gavel from departing House Speaker Michael Madigan to Welch six years ago.</p><p>Several House Democrats also tell me they want no more to do with Welch’s top campaign staff, consultants, etc. Members have been complaining about that problem for at least a couple of years now, and the problem and disagreements seem to be growing.</p><p>The four House Democrats argued in their letter that the chamber needs a new leader who can build consensus.</p><p>“New leadership must work thoughtfully and conscientiously to build a consensus for how we can best serve the needs of the people of Illinois.”</p><p>The current system automatically enforces consensus from above by, among other things, requiring members to prove they have locked up 60 floor votes before they can move to the actual floor.</p><p>Frankly, I’m having a difficult time finding disagreement with any of this stuff. Stop repeating mistakes is never bad advice.</p><p>My assistant Isabel compiled some numbers last week and found that the Democratic caucus will have at least 52 women out of 83-84 members (depending on who wins) when everyone is sworn in for another General Assembly.</p><p>Illinois has never had a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/06/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-steps-down-female-replacement-contenders" target="_blank" >woman speaker.</a> The last two speakers were damaged by staff/member sexual harassment allegations.</p><p>I think Katz Muhl, one of the four letterpeople (sorry, it’s the only moniker I could come up with), has a sound approach.</p><p>Katz Muhl told Isabel she was looking forward to a “robust process” of selecting a new speaker. </p><p>“There are so many talented senior leaders in our caucus. I think about people who have mentored new legislators, who have taught us how to negotiate better, how to build coalitions.” She then added, “and I especially think about women.”</p><p>Rep. Natalie Manley, D-Joliet, a Welch letter signatory, said the gender of the next speaker wasn’t that important to her. “Whether we chose a man or woman doesn’t matter, what matters is character and the ability to work with every member and to make difficult decisions that are necessary for the good of the entire state.”</p><p>Both can be right, and I think they are.</p><p>The House Black Caucus has for years had enough votes to block any bill from passage if members stuck together. But the Black Caucus may have lost its internal veto power.</p><p>The Black Caucus will be picking up two new districts come January, giving it 24 seats, according to Isabel’s count. Mary Catherine Roberson flipped a Republican seat by Danville as did George McClellan in the Metro East.</p><p>McClellan has close ties to Assistant Majority Leader Jay Hoffman, who ran for speaker the last time around and is not exactly a strong Welch ally. Black Caucus member Canty is among the four who want a new speaker to be independent from the current speaker.</p><p>All 24 Black Caucus votes, which probably can’t all be secured anyway, still wouldn’t be enough to stop a new speaker if the House Dems end up with 84 seats.</p><p>The only faction that looks big and cohesive enough to stop a new speaker from being rammed through is the 26 members who signed that Welch letter.</p><p>Of course, some outside groups like labor organizations might try to intervene for or against someone, but involving oneself too closely in this extremely internal task is fraught with risk — just ask Gov. JB Pritzker if he’d repeat his failed involvement in the last Senate president’s race.</p><p>In other words, everyone is going to have to work together.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-870000" name="module-870000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Partner's 8-year-old rules the roost
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been with my significant other for five years and have helped raise his daughter, "Maeve," since she was a toddler. She is now 8, and her behavior — and his enabling — are pushing me to my breaking point. Maeve demands her father do everything for her, including bathing and dressing her, and he complies. She runs around the house in her underwear, which he excuses by saying she is "little enough."</p><p>Maeve's need to be the center of attention extends to everyone; she constantly interrupts adult conversations, and if her father and I are hugging or sitting together, she physically throws herself between us. Furthermore, she throws two-hour tantrums to sleep in our primary bedroom, forcing me to sleep in another room.</p><p>He constantly caves to her demands, scolding her but immediately giving her exactly what she wants. Because I maintain boundaries, she behaves well for me and my older children when her dad isn't around. With him, however, she believes she gets to dictate his actions, bossing him around endlessly and screaming "NO!" right in his face.</p><p>My nerves are shot, and I frequently have to escape outside just to avoid the daily screaming. Am I wrong for feeling Maeve's father is failing her by not teaching her basic independence and discipline? Am I the bad guy here? — <i>DREADING COMING HOME</i></p><p><b>DEAR DREADING:</b> You are not the bad guy — not even close. The fact that Maeve treats you with respect when her dad isn't around shows that she knows how she's supposed to behave. I commend you for that, because it sounds like you're the only one teaching this little girl any manners.</p><p>Sit down with your S.O. and calmly tell him how Maeve's tantrums and manipulative behavior make you feel. Highlight the incidents when you were forced out of your own bed, and describe your hesitation to enter your own home. It is not OK or normal for an 8-year-old to terrorize a parent figure in those ways.</p><p>Because this has gone on so long and Dad still hasn't learned how to discipline his child, it's time to consult a licensed family therapist to address these problems. If your S.O. refuses, you can still benefit by going alone. In the end, you must decide whether you consider Maeve's behavior a deal-breaker in terms of your relationship with her dad.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been invited to a shower and wedding for a great-niece I adore. Would it be appropriate to give her some of my treasured serving pieces as a shower gift? They are much nicer than anything I can now afford to buy her. I am elderly and on a pretty tight budget. — <i>HAPPY FOR HER IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR HAPPY:</b> You have nothing to worry about. To give your great-niece your fine heirloom items would be a lovely and meaningful gesture, especially if you include a card with them explaining their significance and wishing her as much success when she uses them as they have given you.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: What's your message to Democrats as they prepare to take control of Congress? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers for their message to Democrats as they prepare to take control of the U.S. House and Senate. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Don't ---- it up. Take care of your constituents, work with your colleagues in Congress, be decent."<br><i>— Phoebe M.</i></p><p>"Keep Trump out of the spotlight. Ignore him; he likes attention, good or bad. Don't play into his hand." <br><i>— Dean Martin</i></p><p>"Start with not making Jeffries and Schumer majority leaders."<br><i>— Russell Vlk</i></p><p>"Get rid of tariffs. Get out of Iran. Pass a major ethics bill."<br><i>— Jacob Palka</i></p><p>"Jobs, healthcare, food, housing and security. Then impeach."<br><i>— Jeff Mossy Cade</i></p><p>"Stop with your hate for Trump, and fix Social Security before it's too late."<br><i>— Marjorie Hobbs</i></p><p>"Pass universal healthcare. Even a majority of Republicans want it. Call it 'Trump Care' so he signs it. Then just change the name later."<br><i>— Johnny Silva Schaefer</i></p><p>"Investigate the corruption but focus more on passing legislation that helps struggling people."<br><i>— Tom Corcoran</i></p><p>"Don’t go to extremes. Not everybody in this country is a radical."<br><i>— John Rehmer</i></p><p>"Don't waste time on impeachments and so-called investigations that won't go anywhere. ... Better to focus on the things like lower gas and food prices."<br><i>— Drew Pekala</i></p><p>"End tariffs. Get us out of a stupid war. Help lower gas prices and groceries. Make healthcare affordable again."<br><i>— Sharon Costanza</i></p><p>"Create a concrete plan to lower prices and inflation. Reinstate the ACA healthcare subsidies, and help hospitals stay open. Stop the corruption. ... Force Homeland Security to follow the Constitution and stop ICE's violent actions against Americans and others."<br><i>— Doris Noriega</i></p><p>"Stop healthcare from being a for profit enterprise. Make healthcare doable again."<br><i>— Julie Hurt</i></p><p>"Multitask. Do. It. All."<br><i>— Don Anderson</i></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times staff

entries.title: The Bulls offense needs more than a few fixes to get off life support
entries.summary: <p>Everything looks hard for the Bulls offense.</p><p>That’s because it is.</p><p>Tiago Splitter’s gang will enter the Sunday afternoon brunch with Philadelphia with the third-lowest offensive efficiency in the league, the second-worst field goal percentage (41.2%), and the lowest three-point percentage (27.2%).</p><p>Well, the pace is good. The only statistic the Bulls sit atop the league in. But all that means is Splitter has a roster that is really fast at getting off bad shots.</p><p>No wonder players are starting to have those “I got to get mine” moments.</p><p>“My game is in transition so I’m going to take occasional transition threes just to see what it’s like, but really it’s just working the game and trying to be aggressive, pick my spots and try to get everyone involved,” veteran Norman Powell said when asked about his coach publicly not loving some of the threes he’s taken early in the shot clock. “I don’t see myself shooting on like five-straight possessions. That’s not good basketball either. If I’m getting downhill, getting to the basket, getting the shots we want, it's fine.”</p><p>Even rookie Caleb Wilson came out of the loss in New York wanting the ball in his hands more than it was on his way to easily his worst game of the season – a 2-for-12, five-point performance.</p><p>“(Against the Knicks) I didn’t really get the ball much to start the game so I couldn’t really do anything to be aggressive, but when I get the chance to, hopefully I can be aggressive and start opportunities for myself and the others,” the No. 4 overall pick said, trying to be politically correct after a soft benching midway through the third quarter by his coach.</p><p>So what are the immediate answers for the Bulls to start fixing an offense that appears broken?</p><p>One, play better on the defensive end.</p><p>As bad as the offense has looked, the Bulls have the worst defensive efficiency in the Association through their first eight games. It’s not easy to play up-tempo when they are constantly inbounding the ball because they can’t get stops.</p><p>“It’s hard when we’re taking the ball out of the basket every possession, having to play in the halfcourt and try and manufacture things that way,” Powell reiterated. “We need to get stops, get in transition and find easy ways to put the ball in the basket.”</p><p>That’s why it might be time for Splitter to start re-thinking the starting lineup. Nic Claxton (hamstring) will change things a bit, scheduled to make his season debut on Sunday after a hamstring sidelined him early in training camp.</p><p>That will give Splitter another rim protector, more so than Jalen Smith, but Claxton doesn’t stretch the floor like Smith and isn’t much of a difference in the rebound department.</p><p>Splitter has been staggering Josh Giddey with the second unit and Tre Jones a bit more the last few games and that’s had some moments but doesn’t fix the issues with the starters.</p><p>Option No. 1 should be starting Isaac Okoro along with Claxton, Wilson, Powell and Giddey, moving Matas Buzelis with the second unit.</p><p>Okoro will help in the defensive stops department, but more importantly it will allow Buzelis to be a primary scorer with the reserves, getting back to the actions he was in last year – specifically pick-and-rolls – that have often now been given to Wilson this season.</p><p>For most NBA players, it’s a higher priority to close, and Splitter can figure out that group from game-to-game. Plus, maybe it gets Buzelis finding a rhythm and getting into a much-needed flow.</p><p>Whatever Splitter decides he might want to do it quickly. It does feel like the Bulls offense is at rock bottom and can’t get any worse … or can it?</p>
entries.author: Joe Cowley

entries.title: New Blackhawks enforcer Dillon Boucher followed improbable route to NHL: 'I thought about quitting'
entries.summary: <p>RALEIGH, N.C. — Like most people in Rockford, hockey journeyman Dillon Boucher was fast asleep at 11:30 p.m. Monday night.</p><p>He was awakened by his IceHogs linemate and roommate, Connor Mylymok, pounding on his door.</p><p>"I had no idea what was going on," Boucher recalled Saturday. "I thought I was late for practice. </p><p>"But [then Rockford general manager Mark Bernard] called me and said, 'You can't have your phone on silent because I wouldn't be able to tell you you're getting called up.'"</p><p>The 29-year-old forward's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> debut Wednesday against the Panthers completed what has to be one of the most improbable paths to the NHL in recent history.</p><p>Since going undrafted in 2015 (theoretically his first year eligible), Boucher has played two seasons of Canadian major junior hockey, one season of Canadian junior A hockey (the tier below major junior), four seasons of Canadian college hockey, two seasons in the ECHL (the pro league below the AHL) and a little over one season in the AHL.</p><p>"If you had asked me three or four years ago if I was going to be here, I would probably say no," he said. "I'd probably laugh in your face."</p><p>Only three players had ever gone from Dalhousie University in Halifax, Nova Scotia, to the NHL, and none of those three played more than one season at Dalhousie before their ascensions began. So one can understand why Boucher didn't foresee this future.</p><p>"My third year in university, I was going to call it quits," he said. "I was playing in a league...[where] I kept getting suspended for hitting guys. I just wasn't really having fun, and I thought about quitting. I talked to some guys, and they were like, 'You're doing something you love to do. Just stick with it for a while.'</p><p>"When I finished university, my buddy called me and was like, 'Do you want to come try pro? Just play 10 games and see how you like it.' I agreed, and then I never looked back."</p><p>It turned out his unapologetically physical style and eagerness to drop gloves translated better to pro hockey.</p><p>Over the last three seasons combined — including two in Wichita, Kansas, and one in Rockford — he scored only 17 goals but racked up 338 penalty minutes.</p><p>"I haven't gotten suspended yet," he added. "It's a pretty tough league down in university, but they push for school first, so they don't want guys getting injured. [At] the pro level, the refs let stuff go a little more, so it works out in my favor."</p><p>His AHL contract was upgraded to a two-way NHL contract on July 1. And during three preseason appearances for the Hawks, he not only buried a rare goal but also caught coach Jeff Blashill's eye.</p><p>When the Hawks needed another forward for this road trip and Nick Lardis wasn't available — due to a lower-body injury is expected to sideline him for a couple weeks — Boucher got the call. With it, he got an all-time fun fact to tell his grandchildren: he technically replaced Patrick Kane.</p><p>"He knows how to manage a game," Blashill said. "He knows how to get pucks in [and] get pucks out. He’s accountable defensively. And then he brings that physicality and toughness that every team desires and we wanted."</p><p>While frequently reminding himself that he's just in a different league, not playing a different sport, Boucher has come in and done his thing. </p><p>He recorded nine hits against the Panthers and Lightning, and his duel <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/05/blackhawks-lightning-arvid-soderblom-backup-goalie" >Thursday</a> against Lightning enforcer Jeff Viel was arguably the most spirited, intense and vicious Hawks fight in years.</p><p>By Saturday, he dismissed the many stitches and dark bruises surrounding his right eye as "nothing I haven't had before."</p><p>"Some guys like scoring their first goals," he said. "For me, it was the first fight that was special."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="fr" dir="ltr">Boucher vs Viel HUGE TILT <a href="https://t.co/92b7tFimSO">pic.twitter.com/92b7tFimSO</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2118511837381525877?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 6, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Physicality wanted</b></h3><p>Three of the most common critiques of the Hawks by people around the hockey world this season is that they aren't tough enough, aren't physical enough and aren't difficult enough to play against.</p><p>Boucher adds some of those elements, but considering he only plays about eight minutes per game, it's even more important that other Hawks step up.</p><p>"I'm trying to be more physical right from the start of the puck drop," young center Ryan Greene said. "That translates over to every other aspect of the game, too, just [by] being harder. I'm trying to get my body involved as much as I can."</p><p>Connor Bedard, meanwhile, said the Hawks had a conversation following their loss in Detroit last week about "trying to win some more battles." That often requires being more physical, even if they're not precisely the same thing.</p><p>And Bedard, for one, seems to have taken that message to heart, even if not every Hawk has.</p><p>"It just brings us into the fight — all of us — when we're all playing physical and battling and whatnot," Bedard said.</p><p>The Hawks entered Saturday ranked 28th in the NHL in hits (287), despite the fact they don't possess the puck that much and therefore should have more opportunities to dish out hits than the average team.</p><p>"It's a lot more difficult to play against a team that has four lines that are hitting," Boucher said. "I'm going to bring it every night, so if one guy has a night off, I'll try to bring it even more. But when you have four lines that can rub [defensemen] out and make them look over their shoulder twice, you can be a lot more successful."</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Chicago families kick off holiday season with MSI tree lighting festival
entries.summary: <p>More than 40 years ago, Bernadette McGonagle brought her 4-year-old daughter to the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry to see the Christmas trees and kick off the holiday season.</p><p>She never imagined the visit would become an annual tradition, one her family continued every year since.</p><p>“I just always look forward to doing the things that we always do,” McGonagle, 66, said.</p><p>McGonagle and her family kept the tradition alive Saturday, returning to the museum for its annual Tree Lighting and Cultural Festival.</p><p>Her daughter, Jackie Lagonie, carried on the tradition with her own son, Jimmy, after he was born. Dressed in Christmas sweaters and shirts, the family eagerly awaited the moment the museum lit its four-story tree.</p><p>“We just love Christmas,” Lagonie, 44, said “And we love seeing the trees. Seeing what’s changed over the years.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b80000" designated country.</p><p>The tree lighting was also followed by cultural performances, including traditional dances from Colombia, Ireland and Scotland.</p><p>Lagonie said the family always makes a point of searching for the trees representing Ireland, Germany and Denmark — countries tied to their heritage.</p><p>Among the visitors were Jocelyn Aranda and Jose Alvarado, who brought their </figure> </div> </div><p>As the family walked through the exhibit, they pointed out their favorite decorations and said they were considering making the visit an annual tradition of their own.</p><p>“We have always loved Christmas but I think now it's even more fun celebrating because we have [Camila],” Aranda, 32, said. “It's more magical now. So we're trying to do all the Christmas activities we can now.”</p><p>The family, who is Mexican, said they’re raising their daughter to be proud of her heritage. But they also look forward to seeing her grow up and learn about other cultures.</p><p>“I think it's good for her to kind of see other cultures being represented and get a feel for how other people celebrate the holidays,” Alvarado said.</p><p>Chihling Chang and her family waited in the front row for the tree lighting, saying they take the holiday season very seriously.</p><p>Chang said she looks forward to Christmas every year and considers the tree lighting the official start of her family's holiday celebrations. The holiday also gives them an opportunity to gather with family and friends and spend time together, she said.</p><p>But Chang said the family is also a big fan of the museum and wouldn't have missed the chance to see the trees.</p><p>“If they're combining my favorite holiday and my favorite museum, I'm here,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"
